analysis.one_liner: Bans offshore oil and gas drilling off North Carolina's Outer Banks until the science is adequate.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 1990 and referred to the Senate Energy Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from issuing new leases, approving exploration plans, or allowing any drilling for oil or gas on the seafloor off North Carolina's coast. It would have suspended existing leases and kept new leases off the table until January 1, 2000, with the ban lifting only after the Interior Secretary certified — with advice from a new scientific review panel — that enough oceanographic, ecological, and economic data existed to make informed decisions. The bill also ordered federal studies to fill the information gaps and authorized up to $500,000 for them.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal North Carolina communities and workers whose livelihoods depend on fishing and tourism, which the bill's findings value at more than $1 billion a year and identify as vulnerable to disruption from offshore oil development. It would also protect the Outer Banks environment, which the bill describes as exceptionally fragile, from oil spills whose behavior in the area's poorly understood currents could not be reliably predicted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: North Carolina fishing and tourism communities

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits new oil and gas leases offshore North Carolina until January 1, 2000, and suspends active leases for the duration of the ban [S3].

Blocks approval of exploration plans and drilling permits until the Interior Secretary certifies, based on findings of a new Environmental Sciences Review Panel, that adequate information exists [S2] [S3].
Finds that commercial and recreational fishing off North Carolina generates over $1 billion annually and that tourism is the coast's major industry, both at risk from offshore development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies interested in exploring and drilling off North Carolina, notably Mobil Oil, which had a 1989 agreement with the state and Interior to pursue exploration. The government would also spend up to $500,000 on new environmental studies, and the nation forgoes potential offshore energy development in the area.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies seeking Atlantic offshore leases

drawbacks.text: The ban would lock out domestic oil and gas development off North Carolina even if reserves proved significant, running against the national interest in energy production that the bill itself acknowledges the President weighed in other states [S3].

Existing leaseholders would have their active leases suspended without compensation addressed in the bill, and the review-and-studies process could keep the moratorium in place indefinitely beyond 2000 for leases issued later [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a region whose fishing and tourism economy tops $1 billion a year and whose offshore currents were, by the bill's own findings, too poorly understood to predict where a spill would go, the cost of a moratorium fell mostly on oil companies with unproven prospects. The trade-off is heavily on the side of protection, though it does sacrifice potential domestic energy development and imposes study costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1990, sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and stayed there until the Congress ended in January 1991 — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Senator Terry Sanford introduced the Outer Banks Protection Act on July 13, 1990 [S5] [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which took no further action [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in committee without coming to a vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies interested in exploring off North Carolina benefited from the status quo, since no moratorium was enacted and the existing lease and exploration process continued. Coastal communities got no new protection.

for.name: Sen. Terry Sanford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its complete findings on the fishing, tourism, and oceanographic stakes, and saw it referred to committee [S5] [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 13, 1990 and never held a hearing or reported it out [S5].

against.name: Mobil Oil Company
against.role: Oil company pursuing exploration offshore North Carolina
against.what_they_did: Was operating under a 1989 memorandum of understanding with North Carolina and the Interior Department to advance offshore exploration; the bill cited its draft environmental report as insufficient [S3].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan split shows up in the record; the bill's only patron was a Democratic senator in a Democratic-majority Senate, and the committee that held it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have barred new leases, exploration plans, and drilling off North Carolina until 2000 and suspended active leases, directly blocking companies like Mobil from developing prospects off the Outer Banks. Drilling there risked oil spills in poorly understood currents that could damage a $1 billion fishing and tourism economy.

industries.industry: North Carolina commercial and recreational fishing
industries.note: The bill's findings value fishing at over $1 billion a year and note it could be harmed by drilling activity and spills, including exclusion zones around rigs and effects on juvenile fish. The moratorium would protect that economic base.
The findings identify tourism as the coast's major industry and vulnerable to disruption by offshore oil development; the ban would shield the Outer Banks' appeal and environment.
